set1.q: Which is first-line drug therapy for symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Adenosine is used for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is treated first with a beta blocker.
Correct. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is treated first with a beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol.
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia starts with a beta blocker.
Digoxin is not named for ventricular tachycardia. A beta blocker such as metoprolol or carvedilol is the first drug.

set1.q: What separates pulseless electrical activity from asystole?
opts: Correct. Pulseless electrical activity shows an electrocardiogram on which you would expect a pulse, such as normal sinus rhythm, but no perfusing beats; asystole shows nothing.
A flat line with no rate, rhythm, P waves or QRS is asystole itself. Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm without a pulse.
Chaotic, uncoordinated activity without a pulse is ventricular fibrillation. Pulseless electrical activity is organized.
A wide rhythm with a pulse
A rhythm with a pulse is not an arrest rhythm. Pulseless electrical activity is an organized rhythm with no pulse.

set1.q: Which premature ventricular contraction burden puts a patient in the high-risk group?
opts: A single ectopic beat is common and benign. The high-risk burden is over 15% of beats, or 15,000 a day.
A burden of 0.5% is low and calls for reassurance when the heart is normal. The high-risk burden is over 15% of beats.
One percent is the low-burden line: under 1% (or 1,000 a day) with no heart disease and no symptoms is low risk. High risk starts above 15%.

Correct. A high burden, over 15% of beats or 15,000 a day, is one of the high-risk features, with premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy, structural or conduction disease and syncope.

set1.q: Which electrolyte disturbances are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Low calcium and high sodium are not the named triggers. The list is hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia.
Phosphate and chloride are not named. The electrolyte triggers listed are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia.
Correct. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, along with hypercalcemia, are the electrolyte imbalances named as causes of premature ventricular contractions.
Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia are not the named triggers. Low potassium, low magnesium and high calcium are listed.

set1.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the slower rate lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.

set1.q: In third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block, which symptom is associated with an increased risk of sudden death?
opts: Correct. Syncope is a particularly important symptom in complete heart block because it is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
Fatigue and exertional intolerance are common in complete block, but syncope is the symptom specifically tied to an increased risk of sudden death.
Palpitations are not the warning symptom singled out. Syncope in complete block is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
Edema reflects heart failure symptoms, which can occur, but syncope is the symptom linked to an increased risk of sudden death.

set1.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS to time against. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated, even with a pulse.
Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a transitional state that needs defibrillation.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even if the patient looks well.

set1.q: In an elderly patient, which cause tops the list for both Mobitz type II and complete atrioventricular block?
opts: Lyme carditis is a named cause, but in the elderly the most common cause of Mobitz type II and complete block is degenerative His-Purkinje disease.
Long QT syndrome predisposes to torsades de pointes, not to atrioventricular block. Degenerative His-Purkinje disease is the leading cause.
Correct. Acquired disease of the His-Purkinje and conduction system, especially degenerative change from old age with chronic hypertension and diabetes, is the most common cause of both.
Increased vagal tone causes first-degree and Mobitz type I block at the node, often in well-conditioned people. It does not top the list for Mobitz type II or complete block.

set1.q: Which procedure is a named cause of Mobitz type I block?
opts: Pericardiocentesis drains pericardial fluid and is not a named cause of Mobitz type I. Cardiac ablation, which can injure the conduction system, is listed.
An echocardiogram images the heart from the chest wall and cannot injure the conduction system. Cardiac ablation is the procedure named as a cause of Mobitz type I.
Correct. Cardiac ablation is listed among the causes of Mobitz type I block, along with increased vagal tone, atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs, Lyme carditis and ischemia after infarction.
Coronary angiography is a diagnostic procedure and is not a named cause of Mobitz type I. Cardiac ablation is the procedure listed.

set1.q: Which is the most common cause of first-degree atrioventricular block?
opts: Increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve can prolong the PR interval, yet age-related degeneration of the conduction system is the most common cause.
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system is the most common cause: the pathway wears out, so the impulse takes longer to cross the atrioventricular node.
Lyme disease is a named infectious cause of first-degree block, but it is far less common than age-related degeneration of the conduction system.
Atrioventricular node ischemia, usually after a myocardial infarction, is a recognized cause, but the most common cause is age-related degenerative change.

set1.q: Which two arrest rhythms are shockable?
opts: Correct. Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are treated with defibrillation; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are unshockable.
Asystole has no electrical activity to reset and is unshockable. Fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are the shockable pair.
Pulseless electrical activity and asystole are both unshockable and are treated with compressions and epinephrine.
Pulseless electrical activity is unshockable. The shockable pair is ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

set1.q: For an adult with rare premature ventricular contractions, a normal heart and no symptoms, which care strategy fits?
opts: An implantable defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal rhythms. Rare benign premature beats need only reassurance.
Correct. Low-risk adults with a low burden (under 1% or 1,000 a day), no structural heart disease and no symptoms are reassured and helped to eliminate triggers.
A beta blocker is first-line only for symptomatic low-risk patients. Silent, rare premature beats need reassurance and trigger avoidance.
Ablation is reserved for refractory symptoms or beat-induced cardiomyopathy, not for rare silent premature beats.

set1.q: Which chronic pulmonary vascular condition is a named cause of right bundle branch block?
opts: Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause of right bundle branch block, along with age-related degeneration, ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathies and inflammatory or infiltrative disease.
A pleural effusion is fluid around the lung, not a pulmonary vascular disease. Pulmonary hypertension is the named chronic cause.
Sleep apnea is not on the list of causes. Pulmonary hypertension, which strains the right ventricle, is named.
ruled out by a stated finding
A solitary pulmonary nodule is a lung finding, not a pulmonary vascular disease, and does not strain the right ventricle. Pulmonary hypertension is the named chronic cause.

set1.q: What is a Stokes-Adams attack?
opts: Palpitations felt pounding in the neck
Palpitations felt in the neck are described with premature ventricular contractions. A Stokes-Adams attack is a sudden faint from low cerebral blood flow.
Exertional chest pain relieved by rest
Chest pain on exertion that eases with rest describes stable angina. A Stokes-Adams attack is a sudden faint or seizure from falling brain perfusion.
Seizure caused by low blood glucose
A hypoglycemic seizure is metabolic. A Stokes-Adams attack is a faint or seizure caused by a sudden drop in blood flow to the brain from the heart block.
Sudden faint from low brain blood flow
Correct. A Stokes-Adams attack is a sudden fainting spell or seizure from a rapid, temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, a complication of Mobitz type II block.

set1.q: Which chronic condition is a named cause of left bundle branch block?
opts: Pulmonary hypertension strains the right ventricle and is a named cause of right bundle branch block, not left. Chronic systemic hypertension heads the left bundle branch block list.
Hepatitis is not on the list. Chronic hypertension and chronic ischemic heart disease are named causes of left bundle branch block.
Migraine is not a named cause. Chronic hypertension is listed first among the causes of left bundle branch block.
Correct. Chronic hypertension heads the list of causes of left bundle branch block, followed by chronic ischemic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, aortic stenosis and Lenègre-Lev disease.

set1.q: Which parasitic infection is a named cause of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Giardiasis is an intestinal infection that does not reach the conduction system. Chagas disease is the parasitic cause named for complete block.
Correct. Chagas disease is listed among the causes of complete block, with Lyme carditis, bacterial endocarditis with an abscess and inflammatory or infiltrative disease.
Malaria is not a named cause of complete block. The parasitic infection listed is Chagas disease.
Toxoplasmosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease is the parasitic cause named.

set1.q: For an elderly patient with Mobitz type II block found incidentally and causing no symptoms, which plan is appropriate?
opts: A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and is itself a cause of block. Mobitz type II is treated with a permanent pacemaker.
Correct. Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block, and the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Reassurance fits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block. Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms.
Waiting a year ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete block and sudden death. A permanent pacemaker is the plan.

set1.q: Which history places a patient with premature ventricular contractions in the high-risk group?
opts: Young age is not a high-risk feature. Prior syncope, a high burden, cardiomyopathy or structural disease define high risk.
Anxiety is not on the high-risk list. A history of syncope is one of the features that make a patient high risk.
Correct. High-risk features are a burden over 15%, premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy, pre-existing structural or conduction disease and a history of syncope.
Caffeine is a trigger to remove, not a high-risk feature. A history of syncope places the patient in the high-risk group.

set1.q: Why are amiodarone and procainamide avoided in torsades de pointes?
opts: Correct. Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT interval, which would worsen the substrate of torsades; magnesium is the treatment instead.
Lowering magnesium is not the stated reason. They are avoided because they prolong the QT interval.
PR effects are not the issue. Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT, which worsens torsades.
Hypertension is not the reason. These antiarrhythmics are avoided because they prolong the QT interval.

set1.q: What is ventricular bigeminy?
opts: An ectopic beat every third beat is trigeminy. Bigeminy is an ectopic beat every other beat.
Two P waves for every QRS describes a 2:1 atrioventricular block, not an ectopic pattern. Bigeminy alternates normal and ectopic beats.
Three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions make ventricular tachycardia. Bigeminy is an ectopic beat every other beat.
Correct. When every other beat is an ectopic beat the pattern is bigeminy; when every third beat is ectopic it is trigeminy.

set1.q: Which electrocardiogram pattern defines Mobitz type II block?
opts: Long constant PR, no dropped beats
A long, constant PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree block. Mobitz type II drops QRS complexes without warning.
Constant PR with random dropped QRS
Correct. Mobitz type II looks regular apart from random missing QRS complexes; the PR interval of the conducted beats stays constant at 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.
PR lengthens until a QRS drops
A PR interval that progressively lengthens before a dropped beat is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach). Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR.
P waves unrelated to the QRS
P waves fully dissociated from the QRS complexes, at two separate rates, are complete (third-degree) block rather than Mobitz type II.

set1.q: Which is the management of asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Antiarrhythmics are kept for symptomatic episodes when other options fail. Asymptomatic episodes call for optimizing the underlying disease.
Cardioversion treats sustained, unstable tachycardia. Asymptomatic non-sustained runs are managed by optimizing underlying disease.
Correct. Asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is managed by optimizing treatment of the underlying cardiac comorbidities.
Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia by itself is not an indication for a defibrillator. Asymptomatic episodes call for optimizing underlying disease.

set1.q: Why are beta blockers avoided in drug-induced torsades de pointes?
opts: Beta blockers are not avoided for causing hypokalemia. The concern is bradycardia, which indirectly lengthens the QT.
They shorten the QT too much
Beta blockers do not dangerously shorten the QT. By slowing the rate they indirectly prolong it.
No interaction with magnesium is the reason. Beta blockers slow the rate and so indirectly prolong the QT.
Correct. Beta blockers cause bradycardia and lengthen the R to R interval, which indirectly prolongs the QT and worsens acquired torsades.

set1.q: Which statement about shocking asystole and pulseless electrical activity is accurate?
opts: Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are unshockable.
Shock if the line is flat
Shocking a flat line is a television myth: asystole has no electrical activity to reset and is unshockable, as is pulseless electrical activity. Chest compressions start immediately.
Shock if the rhythm is organized
Pulseless electrical activity is already an organized rhythm, so shocking it achieves nothing; it and asystole are both unshockable, and compressions start immediately.
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity and asystole are unshockable; chest compressions start immediately, with epinephrine and early intubation.

set1.q: Which external device detects and shocks fatal ventricular arrhythmias while worn on the body?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing pads pace a slow heart in an emergency. The wearable defibrillator vest is the worn device that shocks.
Correct. There is a wearable (external) cardioverter defibrillator, worn as a vest, that detects fatal ventricular arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
A loop recorder is implanted and only records the rhythm. The wearable cardioverter defibrillator vest is the external device that shocks.
ruled out by a stated finding
A Holter monitor records the rhythm for a day or two but cannot shock. The wearable defibrillator vest detects and shocks fatal rhythms.

set1.q: Above which PR interval do symptoms of first-degree atrioventricular block usually begin to appear?
opts: A PR interval of 0.12 seconds is the lower limit of normal (0.12 to 0.20 seconds), not a symptom threshold. Symptoms usually start above 0.3 seconds.
A PR interval over 0.20 seconds defines first-degree block, but most such patients have no symptoms. Symptoms usually appear above 0.3 seconds.
Correct. The vast majority of first-degree blocks are asymptomatic; symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, palpitations and chest pain usually appear once the PR interval exceeds 0.3 seconds.
Symptoms do not wait for so extreme a delay. They usually appear once the PR interval is greater than 0.3 seconds.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: What is the prognosis of asystole and pulseless electrical activity?
opts: Both are unshockable, and their prognosis is poor; they are usually end-of-life rhythms.
The prognosis is poor regardless; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are usually end-of-life rhythms.
Correct. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity carry a poor prognosis and are usually end-of-life rhythms; ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms.
Fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia have the best prognosis among arrest rhythms. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are poor.

set1.q: Which is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death?
opts: An accessory pathway can allow dangerous pre-excited rhythms, yet coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition.
Correct. Coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death, even in patients without a history of myocardial infarction.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an important cause in young people, but coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition overall.
Long QT syndrome predisposes to torsades de pointes, but coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden death.

set1.q: When ventricular fibrillation stays refractory to shocks after an antiarrhythmic, which drug may be considered?
opts: Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for atrial rhythms and has no place in arrest. Lidocaine may be considered.
Metoprolol is not the next drug in shock-refractory arrest. Lidocaine is considered after amiodarone.
Adenosine is for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Lidocaine may be considered in shock-refractory fibrillation.
Correct. Lidocaine is considered for ventricular fibrillation that remains refractory to shocks after amiodarone.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: Once stabilized after unstable ventricular tachycardia, what do most patients need?
opts: Correct. Once stabilized, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.
A pacemaker treats slow conduction. Survivors of unstable ventricular tachycardia need a defibrillator for secondary prevention.
Magnesium treats torsades acutely. Most survivors of unstable ventricular tachycardia need an implantable defibrillator.
Survivors remain at risk of sudden death; most need an implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention.

set2.q: Which causes should be checked first in a patient with frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative conduction disease. Premature ventricular contractions come mainly from hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.

Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes, so new frequent premature ventricular contractions call for checking oxygen and electrolytes.

High cholesterol and obesity are coronary risk factors, not the named causes to check. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium) are the causes to look for first.

set2.q: Sudden cardiac death is defined as unexpected natural death from cardiac causes within what time of collapse?
opts: Ten minutes is too short a window. The definition counts unexpected cardiac death within 1 hour of collapse.
Correct. Sudden cardiac death is generally defined as unexpected natural death from cardiac causes occurring within 1 hour of the patient's collapse.
Six hours is not the window used. Sudden cardiac death is death within 1 hour of collapse.
Thirty days is an outcome window, not the definition. Sudden cardiac death occurs within 1 hour of collapse.

opts: A wearable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms; it does not pace a slow escape rhythm. A permanent pacemaker is definitive.
Correct. Emergent transcutaneous pacing bridges the patient, and the definitive treatment for complete heart block is a permanent pacemaker.
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and is itself a cause of block. Complete block is treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker.
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of complete block. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

set2.q: Once an advanced airway is in place during cardiac arrest, how are breaths given with continuous compressions?
opts: A breath every 2 seconds would over-ventilate. The rate is 1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions.
Breaths continue during arrest. With an advanced airway they come at 1 every 6 seconds with continuous compressions.
Correct. Once intubated, cardiopulmonary resuscitation becomes continuous chest compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds.
Pausing for two breaths after 30 compressions is the pattern without an advanced airway. With one, compressions are continuous with 1 breath every 6 seconds.

set2.q: Which electrolyte is given as an intravenous push and then as an infusion to break torsades de pointes?
opts: Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, and more magnesium is then given as an infusion; it is the main treatment.
Low potassium is a cause of a long QT and should be corrected, but the drug that breaks torsades is intravenous magnesium.
Low calcium is a cause of a long QT, yet calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades. Magnesium is.
Phosphate plays no named role in torsades. Intravenous magnesium, then a magnesium infusion, is the treatment.

set2.q: Which degenerative, fibrotic disease of the conduction system is a named cause of left bundle branch block?
opts: Lyme carditis is an infection that causes atrioventricular block. The degenerative, fibrotic conduction disease named for left bundle branch block is Lenègre-Lev disease.
Chagas disease is a parasitic infection named for complete heart block. The fibrotic conduction disease named for left bundle branch block is Lenègre-Lev disease.
Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy is a transient ballooning of the apex. The degenerative conduction disease named here is Lenègre-Lev disease.
Correct. Degenerative or fibrotic disease of the conduction system, Lenègre-Lev disease, is listed among the causes of left bundle branch block.

set2.q: Which finding defines hemodynamic instability in ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Correct. Instability is defined as any one of chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension.
A rate in the tachycardic range is expected and does not by itself define instability. Chest pain, altered mental status, dyspnea or hypotension do.
Palpitations are common and do not define instability. The four markers are chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath and hypotension.
Every ventricular tachycardia has wide complexes. Instability is defined clinically: chest pain, altered mental status, dyspnea or hypotension.

set2.q: Which treatment is used for symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
opts: Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction gets a biventricular pacer.
Ablation destroys tissue and would not restore left ventricular activation. The named treatment is a biventricular pacemaker.
Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which is treated with a biventricular pacer.
Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias with a pulse. It cannot correct a conduction delay; a biventricular pacer resynchronizes the ventricles.

set2.q: Which antiarrhythmic can be used in torsades de pointes?
opts: Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used.
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided. Intravenous lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used.
Beta blockers are avoided because bradycardia lengthens the QT. Lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used.
Correct. Intravenous lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that can be used in torsades, though the evidence for it is limited; magnesium remains the main treatment.

set2.q: Which is the management of asymptomatic Mobitz type I block?
opts: Correct. Mobitz type I needs no treatment unless there are debilitating symptoms or heart failure symptoms; a permanent pacemaker is considered only for symptomatic patients.
A permanent pacemaker is for symptomatic Mobitz type I, or for Mobitz type II even without symptoms. Asymptomatic Mobitz type I needs no treatment.
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergency measure for unstable Mobitz type II or complete block, not for asymptomatic Mobitz type I.
Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic for stable ventricular tachycardia. It is not used for Mobitz type I, which needs no treatment when silent.

set2.q: Which electrocardiogram finding defines first-degree atrioventricular block?
opts: P waves unrelated to the QRS
P waves with no relationship to the QRS complexes describe complete (third-degree) block. In first-degree block each P wave is followed by a QRS.
Correct. First-degree atrioventricular block is a prolonged PR interval, greater than 0.20 seconds and constant, with one P wave for every narrow QRS complex.
PR lengthening until a QRS drops
A PR interval that grows longer until a QRS complex is dropped is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. In first-degree block every P wave conducts.
Constant PR with random dropped QRS
A constant PR interval with random missing QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block. First-degree block has a long PR but never drops a beat.

set2.q: How does Mobitz type I block usually present?
opts: Palpitations felt in the neck are described with premature ventricular contractions. Mobitz type I block usually causes no symptoms at all.
Heart failure symptoms are a reason to treat Mobitz type I, not its usual presentation; most patients are asymptomatic and need no treatment.

Correct. Mobitz type I block is usually asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur they are dizziness, fatigue, exertional intolerance and syncope, and a symptomatic patient is considered for a permanent pacemaker.
Syncope can occur, but it is not the usual picture: Mobitz type I is usually asymptomatic, and a patient who does faint is considered for a permanent pacemaker.

opts: Correct. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin all slow atrioventricular conduction and are named causes of first-degree block.
Furosemide is a loop diuretic that does not slow atrioventricular conduction. The named drug causes are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that acts on vessels; the named calcium channel blockers are the nondihydropyridines, along with beta blockers and digoxin.
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and is not a named cause. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are.

set2.q: Which mechanism makes atrioventricular block more common in elderly patients?
opts: Atrial size is not the stated mechanism. Elderly patients develop block through degenerative change of the conduction system.
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system is the most common cause of first-degree block and drives the His-Purkinje disease behind Mobitz type II and complete block.
Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, but it is not the age-linked mechanism. Degeneration of the conduction system is.
Lyme carditis is an infectious cause at any age, not an age-related mechanism. Elderly patients develop block from degenerative conduction disease.

opts: The size of the rsR' complex does not set therapy. Treatment of right bundle branch block depends on the underlying condition.
Correct. Right bundle branch block is usually asymptomatic, and its treatment depends on the underlying condition; prognosis depends on the presence and type of heart disease.
QRS width confirms the block but does not set treatment. Treatment depends on the underlying condition.
Heart rate is not what guides treatment. Right bundle branch block is managed according to the underlying condition.

opts: Catheter ablation is second-line, used when symptoms are refractory or drug therapy is not tolerated. A beta blocker comes first.
An implantable defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal rhythms. Symptomatic, low-risk premature beats are treated first with a beta blocker.
Correct. In low-risk patients with symptoms, a beta blocker is first-line; catheter ablation is kept for symptoms refractory to it or a patient who cannot tolerate drug therapy.
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic used for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. A beta blocker is first-line for symptomatic low-risk patients.

set2.q: After defibrillation for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, which procedure is urgent?
opts: Ablation is used for premature beats and some ventricular tachycardia, but the urgent step after polymorphic tachycardia is coronary angiography.
Pericardiocentesis drains a tamponade. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is followed by urgent coronary angiography.
Stress testing is not urgent and could be dangerous here. Urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization is the step.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated, followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization, because acute ischemia is its most common cause.

set2.q: Because Mobitz type II block usually originates at the bundle of His, what is true of its escape rhythm?
opts: The sinoatrial node keeps firing, but its impulses are blocked below. The escape rhythm that takes over is weak and unreliable.
A low escape rhythm is slow, not above 60 per minute. With a block at the bundle of His the escape rhythm is weak and unreliable.
Correct. Because the block sits low, at the bundle of His, the escape rhythm is weak and unreliable, which adds to the risk of sudden death.
A fast, narrow escape rhythm would come from higher in the junction. A block at the bundle of His leaves a weak, unreliable escape rhythm.

set2.q: Which arrest rhythms carry the best prognosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation does carry the best prognosis, but asystole has a poor one and is usually an end-of-life rhythm. The best-prognosis pair is ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation.
Ventricular tachycardia does carry the best prognosis, but pulseless electrical activity has a poor one. The best-prognosis arrest rhythms are ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation.
Correct. Among cardiac arrest rhythms, ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation have the best prognosis; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are poor.
Asystole and pulseless electrical activity have a poor prognosis and are usually end-of-life rhythms.

set2.q: Which electrical treatment is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms such as Mobitz type II and complete block. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with unsynchronized defibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, so there is no trial of drugs first: it is defibrillated, and an antiarrhythmic or beta blocker may be added afterward.
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and its QRS shape keeps changing, so it is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present.
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a consistent QRS and suits unstable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse. Polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated.

set2.q: Into which two fascicles does the left bundle branch divide?
opts: Correct. Past the bundle of His the conduction system splits into right and left bundle branches, and the left bundle divides into anterior and posterior fascicles, where a fascicular block can occur.
Right and left name the two bundle branches that leave the bundle of His; the left bundle branch then divides into an anterior and a posterior fascicle.
Inner and outer are not the names of the left bundle's divisions. The left bundle branch divides into an anterior and a posterior fascicle, the sites of a fascicular block.
Medial and apical are not the named divisions. The left bundle branch divides into anterior and posterior fascicles.

set2.q: Which role does non-sustained ventricular tachycardia alone play in the decision to place an implantable defibrillator?
opts: Non-sustained runs alone do not justify a defibrillator; only some patients qualify, for primary prevention of sudden death related to sustained ventricular tachycardia.
Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia does not rule a defibrillator out. Some patients are candidates for primary prevention.
No vest requirement is stated. Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia alone is not an indication for a defibrillator.
Correct. Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia in and of itself is not an indication for a defibrillator, although some patients qualify for one for primary prevention of sudden death.

set2.q: Which complication of bacterial endocarditis is a named cause of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Splinter hemorrhages are a peripheral sign of endocarditis in the nail beds and do not cause block. An abscess near the conduction system does.
Septic emboli to the lungs do not interrupt cardiac conduction. Endocarditis causes complete block when an abscess forms.
Glomerulonephritis affects the kidneys, not the conduction system. The endocarditis complication tied to complete block is an abscess.
Correct. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is listed among the causes of complete block, because the infection can extend into the conduction system.

set2.q: When is catheter ablation used for low-risk patients with symptomatic premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Correct. A beta blocker is first-line; catheter ablation is used when symptoms are refractory or the patient cannot tolerate drug therapy.
Ablation is not first-line in low-risk patients. A beta blocker comes first, and ablation follows if it fails or is not tolerated.
A burden under 1% with no symptoms or heart disease needs only reassurance and removal of triggers, not ablation.
Bigeminy alone is not an indication. Ablation in low-risk patients is for symptoms refractory to, or intolerant of, a beta blocker.

set2.q: When left bundle branch block does cause symptoms, what do they resemble?
opts: Wheezing bronchospasm is not the picture. Symptoms from left bundle branch block resemble a heart failure exacerbation.
Anxiety symptoms are not described. Symptomatic left bundle branch block looks like a heart failure exacerbation with exertional dyspnea.
Low blood glucose is not the comparison. Symptoms resemble a heart failure exacerbation: dizziness, shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion.
Correct. Symptomatic left bundle branch block resembles a congestive heart failure exacerbation, with dizziness, shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion.

set2.q: For premature ventricular contractions under 1% of beats with no structural heart disease and no symptoms, which is the plan?
opts: A beta blocker is first-line only when low-risk patients have symptoms. Silent, low-burden beats need reassurance and removal of triggers.
Ablation is kept for refractory symptoms or cardiomyopathy. Low-burden, silent beats in a normal heart need only reassurance.
An implantable defibrillator is for prevention of sudden death from lethal rhythms, not for occasional benign ectopic beats.
Correct. Low-risk patients with a low burden (under 1% or 1,000 a day), no structural heart disease and no symptoms need reassurance and elimination of triggers.

set2.q: For hemodynamically stable, sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which approach is used?
opts: Adenosine targets atrioventricular nodal rhythms. Stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with an intravenous antiarrhythmic.

Correct. Stable, monomorphic sustained ventricular tachycardia is pharmacologically cardioverted with intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide, after a monitor, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, oxygen and labs.
Defibrillation is for pulseless or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. A stable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse gets an intravenous antiarrhythmic.
Synchronized cardioversion is for the unstable patient who still has a pulse. A stable patient is cardioverted with drugs first.

set2.q: Which infiltrative diseases are named causes of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Asthma and emphysema are lung diseases, not infiltrative heart disease. Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis are the named causes.
Correct. Inflammatory and infiltrative disease, namely myocarditis, amyloidosis and sarcoidosis, is listed among the causes of complete heart block.
Cirrhosis and pancreatitis do not infiltrate the conduction system. Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis are the infiltrative causes named.
Osteoporosis and gout are not named causes. The infiltrative diseases listed for complete block are amyloidosis and sarcoidosis.

set2.q: Which finding in lead V1 is expected in left bundle branch block?
opts: Correct. Left bundle branch block shows a QRS over 0.12 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 (an rS pattern), a monophasic R in the lateral leads and no Q waves in I, V5 and V6.
An rsR' pattern (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 is the hallmark of right bundle branch block, where the right ventricle depolarizes late.
A delta wave is the slurred QRS upstroke of an accessory pathway with pre-excitation. Left bundle branch block gives a dominant S wave in V1.
A tall narrow R wave in V1 is not the pattern. Left bundle branch block widens the QRS and leaves a dominant S wave in V1.

set2.q: In a high-risk patient with premature ventricular contractions but no isolated beat-induced cardiomyopathy, what is the first step?
opts: Correct. Outside isolated premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy, the first step in high-risk patients is a beta blocker and optimized treatment of the underlying cardiac disease.
Reassurance alone is for low-risk, low-burden patients without symptoms. High-risk patients start a beta blocker and optimize their heart disease.
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, not isolated premature beats.
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. High-risk premature beats are treated first with a beta blocker and optimized cardiac care.
